conflicts.name: 2026 Iran war (US and Israel vs Iran)
conflicts.started: 2026-02-28 (US Operation Epic Fury and Israeli Operation Roaring Lion; current phase since ceasefire collapse on 2026-07-08)
conflicts.summary: A US-Israeli air war on Iran that began on 28 February 2026 killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and much of Iran's security leadership. Iran answered with thousands of missiles and drones at Israel, US bases and every Gulf monarchy, and closed the Strait of Hormuz. A June peace memorandum collapsed in July, and by late October the two sides are in an armed stand-off with no ceasefire and threats of a second round after the US midterms.

conflicts.name: Ecuador's war on gangs and the Colombia border dispute
conflicts.started: 2024-01-09 (President Noboa declares an 'internal armed conflict' against criminal groups)
conflicts.summary: Ecuador, once one of South America's safer countries, recorded 8,847 homicides in 2025, its deadliest year, as gangs fought over cocaine export routes through its Pacific ports. Homicides fell 6.4 percent in January to August 2026, mainly in Guayaquil, while violence spread to Machala and dozens of smaller cantons. From March 2026 US forces joined Ecuadorian strikes on Colombian guerrilla-trafficker camps on the border, feeding a tariff war and a war of words with Colombia.

zones.name: Guayaquil and Durán
zones.note: Main cocaine port and the centre of gang warfare; homicides fell in 2026 but remain the highest in absolute terms.

zones.name: Los Ríos province
zones.note: Inland transit province with over 1,100 homicides in 2025.

zones.name: Manabí coast (Manta, Portoviejo)
zones.note: Fishing ports used for cocaine shipments; about 839 homicides in Jan to Aug 2026.

zones.name: El Oro (Machala)
zones.note: Fastest-rising violence in 2026, with Machala homicides up from 207 to 367.

zones.name: Sucumbíos and the Colombian border
zones.note: Comandos de la Frontera camps; joint Ecuador-US air strikes from Mar 2026.

conflicts.name: Fano insurgency in Amhara
conflicts.started: 2023-08-01 (approximate; Fano has fought the federal government since 2023)
conflicts.summary: Fano, a loose network of Amhara militias that fought alongside the government in the 2020 to 2022 Tigray war, has been in revolt since 2023. In 2026 it disrupted the national election, joined a coalition with the TPLF and OLA, and attacked federal supply lines as the army fought in Tigray.

zones.name: North Wollo and the A2 corridor
zones.note: Woldia, Kobo, Lalibela and Wurgessa; Fano attacks on army supply lines to Tigray.

zones.note: Fano attacks on Dabat and the road north to Tigray.

zones.note: Long-running Fano stronghold.

conflicts.name: Haiti's gang war (Viv Ansanm versus the state and the Gang Suppression Force)
conflicts.started: 2024-02-29 (formation of the Viv Ansanm gang coalition)
conflicts.summary: Haiti's armed gangs, united since 2024 in the Viv Ansanm coalition, control most of Port-au-Prince and are expanding into the Artibonite and Centre departments. More than 5,915 people were killed in 2025 and over 3,000 in the first half of 2026, many of them in government operations using explosive drones with help from a US private military company. A UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force began deploying in April 2026, and nearly 1.5 million Haitians are displaced.

zones.name: Port-au-Prince metropolitan area
zones.note: About 80 percent under Viv Ansanm control; drone strikes and police operations in downtown, Delmas and Tabarre.

zones.note: Rival gang clashes killed 463 people in Apr to Jun 2026; GSF ambush at Croix-des-Bouquets in Oct 2026.

conflicts.name: Israel-Hamas war in Gaza (ceasefire phase)
conflicts.started: 2025-10-10 (ceasefire phase of the war that began 2023-10-07)
conflicts.summary: A US-brokered ceasefire has stopped full-scale war in Gaza since 10 October 2025 and returned all hostages, but Israel holds a growing share of the Strip behind the 'Yellow Line' and conducts near-daily strikes. Phase two, which trades Hamas disarmament for further Israeli withdrawal and an international force, is deadlocked.

zones.name: Gaza City (Hamas-held west of line)
zones.note: Largest population concentration; frequent Israeli strikes on operatives; building collapse killed 20+ on 16 Sep 2026.

zones.name: Shuja'iyya and Tuffah (Yellow Line edge)
zones.note: Line markers moved about 295 m west here in late 2025; repeated shootings of people crossing.

conflicts.name: Israel-Hezbollah war in Lebanon (2026)
conflicts.summary: Hezbollah reopened fire on 2 March 2026 after the US-Israeli war on Iran began, and Israel answered with its deepest invasion of Lebanon in a generation, crossing the Litani and taking Beaufort. Since a 19 June ceasefire Israel holds a 570-600 sq km 'security zone' behind its own Yellow Line, while a US-brokered Israel-Lebanon framework asks the Lebanese army to disarm Hezbollah zone by zone.

conflicts.name: Mexico's cartel war (CJNG succession fight and Sinaloa Cartel civil war)
conflicts.started: 2024-09-09 (start of the Sinaloa Cartel civil war; CJNG succession crisis from 2026-02-22)
conflicts.summary: Mexico's war against and among drug cartels entered a new phase when the army killed CJNG leader 'El Mencho' on 22 February 2026, setting off about 250 to 280 burning roadblocks across some 20 states. In Sinaloa, the civil war between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos passed two years in September 2026 with about 3,724 murders and about 4,000 people disappeared. Official national homicide figures have nonetheless fallen by roughly half since 2024.

zones.note: Core battleground of the Chapitos versus Mayos war since Sep 2024; curfews, shootings and disappearances.

conflicts.name: Myanmar civil war
conflicts.started: 2021-02-01 (coup; current phase is the junta counteroffensive under a post-election government, 2025-2026)
conflicts.summary: Five years after the 2021 coup, Myanmar's war has swung back toward the military on several fronts. With China having pushed the strongest northern ethnic armies into ceasefires, the junta, now presented as an elected government under President Min Aung Hlaing, is using air power, drones and river and sea lift to relieve besieged garrisons and retake towns, while the Arakan Army still holds most of Rakhine State.

conflicts.name: Pakistan's insurgencies (TTP and allies in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, BLA in Balochistan)
conflicts.started: 2026-01-31 (current escalation; both insurgencies are long-running)
conflicts.summary: Pakistan is living through its worst militant violence in about five years: the Pakistani Taliban and allied factions wage a daily campaign of bombings and ambushes in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, while the Balochistan Liberation Army mounts large coordinated assaults on cities, trains and security posts. The violence is the main driver of Pakistan's war with the Afghan Taliban, whom Islamabad blames for sheltering the TTP.

conflicts.name: Pakistan-Afghanistan war (Pakistan vs Afghan Taliban)

conflicts.summary: Pakistan and the Taliban government it once backed have fought two rounds of open warfare since October 2025, culminating in Pakistan declaring 'open war' in February 2026 and bombing Kabul, Kandahar and Bagram. After a spring lull, Pakistani air strikes resumed on 21 September 2026 following a deadly militant assault on a police compound in Kohat, and no ceasefire was in place in late October.

conflicts.name: Russia-Ukraine long-range strike war
conflicts.started: 2022-02-24 (energy-grid campaign renewed October 2025)
conflicts.summary: Both sides wage a nightly long-range war. Russia fires hundreds of drones, increasingly jet-powered, plus ballistic and cruise missiles at Ukraine's power grid, cities and ports, while Ukraine hits Russian refineries, arms plants, airbases and ships up to 2,300 km away. Civilian casualties in Ukraine hit a multi-year high in September 2026.

conflicts.name: Russia-Ukraine war (ground war)
conflicts.started: 2022-02-24 (full-scale invasion; war began 2014)
conflicts.summary: Europe's largest war since 1945 entered its fifth year with Russia still attacking along a roughly 1,200 km front but gaining almost nothing in 2026. Russia took Pokrovsk, Myrnohrad, Siversk and Huliaipole in late 2025, then stalled; Ukraine counterattacked in the south from February and north of Lyman from September. ISW assesses Russia has been net losing ground since 1 September 2026, while the battle for Kostiantynivka grinds on a year after it began.

zones.note: Year-long urban battle; Russian 8th Combined Arms Army infiltrating the city, Ukrainian positions still held on the outskirts and in the west.

zones.name: Pokrovsk, Myrnohrad and Dobropillia
zones.note: Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad fell by January 2026; in October 2026 Russian infiltrators reached central Dobropillia.

conflicts.name: Somalia: al-Shabaab insurgency and political crisis
conflicts.started: 2025-02-01 (approximate; al-Shabaab offensive in central Somalia and federal political breakdown)
conflicts.summary: Al-Shabaab, al-Qaeda's Somali affiliate, has retaken ground in central and southern Somalia while the federal government is consumed by disputes with member states and the opposition over the president's expired term. conflicts.name: South Sudan conflict (government vs SPLA-IO)

conflicts.summary: South Sudan's 2018 peace deal has collapsed into renewed war between President Salva Kiir's forces, backed by Ugandan troops, and the SPLA-IO loyal to detained former vice president Riek Machar. Fighting is fiercest in Nuer areas of Jonglei and Upper Nile, where government air strikes have hit civilians, and the country is heading into elections set for 22 December 2026.

conflicts.name: Sudan war (SAF vs RSF)
conflicts.started: 2023-04-15 (current phase: Kordofan war after the fall of El Fasher on 2025-10-26)
conflicts.summary: Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have fought since April 2023 in what the UN calls the world's largest humanitarian crisis. After the RSF captured El Fasher in October 2025 and completed its hold on Darfur, the war moved into Kordofan, where the army counterattacked from July 2026 and broke the RSF ring around El Obeid. Both sides now rely heavily on drones, which the UN says caused most civilian deaths in 2026.

zones.note: RSF holds all five Darfur state capitals since El Fasher fell on 26 Oct 2025; SAF and allied drone strikes hit Nyala, Ed Daein, Kutum and Zalingei.

conflicts.summary: Damascus crushed the Kurdish-led SDF in a three-week offensive in January 2026, absorbed its forces and saw it formally dissolve in August, and the US then left Syria. zones.note: Kurdish districts besieged Oct-Dec 2025, taken by government Jan 2026.

Since taking office on 7 August 2026, President Abelardo de la Espriella has abandoned negotiations in favour of air strikes and a pledge to capture or kill ten group leaders within 90 days. bases.name: Al Udeid Air Base
bases.why: The largest US base in the Middle East and the forward headquarters of US Central Command, home to the Combined Air Operations Center that runs the air war across the region. If you want to know how America fights from the Gulf, this is the nerve center. Its size and symbolism make it Iran's favorite target.
bases.assets: About 10,000 personnel (2026); CENTCOM forward HQ and Combined Air Operations Center; 379th Air Expeditionary Wing with KC-135 tankers, ISR and airlift; RAF detachment.
bases.year: Hit by an Iranian ballistic missile around 3 March 2026 with no casualties reported. On 2 March Qatari F-15s shot down two Iranian Su-24s reportedly heading for the base and Ras Laffan. Also hit in Iran's June 2025 retaliation for US strikes on its nuclear sites. The Pentagon is reportedly weighing whether some Gulf bases are still viable.

bases.name: Al Dhafra Air Base
bases.why: The main US air hub in the UAE, a short hop across the Gulf from Iran and overlooking the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz. It hosts high-value surveillance and tanker aircraft that feed the whole regional air picture, and France keeps its Gulf fighter detachment here.
bases.assets: 380th Air Expeditionary Wing (ISR, tankers, fighters on rotation); UAE Air Force F-16 Block 60 and Mirage 2000-9; French Air Base 104 Rafale detachment.
bases.year: Targeted in Iran's first wave on 28 February 2026; minor structural damage from secondary explosions, and debris killed a civilian near Zayed International Airport. The UAE says it intercepted 537 ballistic missiles, 2,256 drones and 26 cruise missiles by 9 April.

bases.name: Naval Support Activity Bahrain (US Fifth Fleet HQ)
bases.why: Home of the US Fifth Fleet, which runs naval operations from the Gulf through the Arabian Sea to the Red Sea, and headquarters of the multinational Combined Maritime Forces. It is the reason the US Navy can command inside the Gulf rather than from outside it.
bases.assets: HQ US Naval Forces Central Command and Fifth Fleet; Combined Maritime Forces HQ; Mina Salman pier; UK Naval Support Facility nearby.
bases.year: Struck by Iranian missiles and drones on 28 February 2026; two US Defense Department employees wounded on 2 March; more attacks in June were mostly intercepted. The Chief of Naval Operations said 'We're not getting back there anytime soon.'

bases.name: Isa Air Base
bases.why: Bahrain's main military airfield and a staging base for US maritime patrol aircraft that track ships and submarines in the Gulf. It complements the Fifth Fleet headquarters a few kilometers north.
bases.assets: Royal Bahraini Air Force F-16s; rotating US Navy P-8A Poseidon detachments and other US aircraft.
bases.year: Iran claimed a strike on 3 March 2026; satellite imagery showed several P-8 hangars hit on 30 March.

bases.name: Camp Arifjan
bases.why: The US Army's main command and logistics hub in the Middle East, holding prepositioned equipment so armored units can fly in and pick up their gear. Any US ground campaign in the region runs through here.
bases.assets: Forward HQ of US Army Central (ARCENT); Army Prepositioned Stocks; sustainment and logistics units.
bases.year: Kuwait is one of eight countries where a Pentagon Inspector General report says Iranian strikes damaged US base buildings in 2026; open-source compilations did not single out Arifjan itself.

bases.name: Ali Al Salem Air Base
bases.why: Nicknamed 'The Rock', it is the main US airlift hub moving troops and cargo into Iraq, Syria and the Gulf, and a coalition base for Italian and Canadian forces. It shows how much of the coalition's logistics depends on a handful of airfields within missile range of Iran.
bases.assets: 386th Air Expeditionary Wing (airlift and ISR); Italian air task force with MQ-9 Reapers and Eurofighter Typhoons; Canadian contingent at Camp Canada.
bases.year: Hit repeatedly in 2026: drones on 28 February, missiles damaging Canadian bunkers on 2 March, an Italian MQ-9 destroyed and two Italian Typhoons damaged on 15 March, and a 6 April drone strike that reportedly injured 15 Americans.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Ali Al Salem Air Base

bases.name: Camp Buehring
bases.why: Desert staging and training camp near the Iraqi border where rotating US Army brigades and aviation units prepare before moving forward in the region.
bases.assets: Rotational US Army brigade and aviation elements; ranges and staging areas.
bases.year: Hit by an Iranian drone on 1 March 2026; later reporting said an Iranian F-5 fighter got through the defenses and carried out a bombing run, a rare manned-aircraft attack on a US base.

bases.name: Prince Sultan Air Base
bases.why: Deep in the Saudi interior south of Riyadh, it sits farther from Iran than the coastal Gulf hubs and became the main home for the tankers and airborne radar planes that keep a big air campaign running. Lose those support aircraft and the fighters cannot reach their targets.
bases.assets: 378th Air Expeditionary Wing; rotating US fighters; KC-135 tankers; E-3 Sentry AWACS; Royal Saudi Air Force units.
bases.year: Iranian missiles damaged five US tankers in early March 2026, and a late-March strike destroyed or damaged an E-3 Sentry and at least one KC-135 on the ground. US officials said 29 service members were wounded in a single week; one US soldier died after an Iranian missile attack on a US base in Saudi Arabia.

bases.name: Muwaffaq Salti Air Base (Azraq)
bases.why: Jordan's Azraq air base has become one of the most important US fighter bases in the Levant, sitting under the flight path of Iranian missiles and drones heading for Israel. It is the obvious fallback if the US thins out its Gulf bases.
bases.assets: Royal Jordanian Air Force F-16s; rotating US fighter squadrons and drones; coalition aircraft.
bases.year: Jordan took 204 Iranian missiles and drones in two waves on 7 and 14 March 2026, most intercepted. US troops leaving al-Tanf in Syria moved to Jordan in February 2026, and shifting more US infrastructure to Jordan is under discussion.

bases.assets: Large dry dock and naval berths; US access arrangements with Oman; UK Joint Logistics Support Base able to support carriers and submarines.
bases.year: Hit by Iranian drone strikes from 1 March 2026 because US forces use it.

bases.why: Southern Omani port on the Arabian Sea used for US Navy logistics, far from Hormuz and on the approach to the Gulf of Aden and Bab el-Mandeb.
bases.assets: Container and bulk terminals; fuel storage; logistics calls by US and allied ships.
bases.year: Hit by Iranian drones from 1 March 2026, including a fuel tank on 11 March.

bases.name: Ras Laffan Industrial City (LNG)
bases.why: The world's largest LNG export complex, supplying a large share of global liquefied gas to Europe and Asia. It is not a military base, but it is exactly the kind of strategic target that turns a Gulf war into a global energy crisis.
bases.assets: LNG liquefaction trains, gas processing (including Barzan), export berths.
bases.year: QatarEnergy halted all gas production on 2 March 2026 and declared force majeure. An 18 March Iranian strike knocked out about 17% of LNG export capacity, which Qatar's energy minister said could take 3 to 5 years to repair. A 21 June explosion during restart at Barzan killed at least 13 workers.

bases.name: Abqaiq oil processing facility
bases.why: The largest crude oil stabilization plant in the world, processing most of Saudi Arabia's crude before export. The 2019 drone and missile attack here briefly knocked out about half of Saudi output and proved how fragile Gulf energy is to cheap precision weapons.
bases.assets: Crude processing and stabilization plant; pipeline hub feeding Ras Tanura and the East-West pipeline.
bases.year: No confirmed hit on Abqaiq in 2026 in the sources reviewed, but the nearby Ras Tanura refinery was struck by drones on 4 March 2026 and briefly shut, and the Shaybah field was repeatedly targeted.

bases.name: Kharg Island
bases.why: Iran's main crude export terminal, handling the large majority of its oil exports. Whoever controls or threatens Kharg holds Iran's economy hostage, which is why seizing it has been debated in Washington.
bases.assets: Crude loading terminals and storage; IRGC and naval facilities, air defenses, mine and missile storage (per CENTCOM).
bases.year: On 13 March 2026 the US Air Force bombed more than 90 military targets on the island, including mine and missile storage, while deliberately sparing oil infrastructure. Tankers kept loading afterward; a ground seizure was considered but not ordered.

bases.name: Bandar Abbas naval complex
bases.why: Iran's main naval base sits right on the Strait of Hormuz, the launch point for the fast attack craft, mines, submarines and anti-ship missiles that let Iran threaten a fifth of the world's oil. Point is city center; naval facilities line the waterfront.
bases.assets: Iranian Navy HQ for the Gulf; Kilo-class and midget submarines; IRGC fast attack craft; coastal anti-ship missiles.
bases.year: Iran's navy was hammered in the 2026 war: US figures cite 130 to 155 Iranian vessels struck or destroyed, the frigate IRIS Dena was sunk by USS Charlotte around 4 March, and Israel said it killed IRGC Navy commander Alireza Tangsiri. Damage at Bandar Abbas itself was not individually confirmed in the sources reviewed.

bases.name: Chabahar Port (Shahid Beheshti)
operators: Ports and Maritime Organization of Iran
bases.why: Iran's only ocean port outside the Gulf, developed with India as a route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan. It sits about 170 km from China-backed Gwadar, making the Makran coast a quiet India-China rivalry.
bases.assets: Container and bulk terminals operated in part by India Ports Global.

bases.name: Fordow Fuel Enrichment Plant
bases.why: Iran's enrichment plant buried deep inside a mountain near Qom, built to survive airstrikes. It was the reason the US built and used the 30,000-pound GBU-57 bunker buster, and its status is the best single gauge of whether Iran can rebuild a path to weapons-grade uranium.
bases.assets: Underground centrifuge halls (largely destroyed 2025); above-ground support area; air defenses.
bases.year: Largely destroyed by US B-2 strikes in June 2025; all four tunnel entrances were still buried as of mid-May 2026. The support area was hit between 18 and 30 March 2026, and Iran has added earthen chicanes on access roads. No sign of reconstruction of the underground plant as of mid-2026.

bases.name: Natanz Nuclear Facility
bases.why: Iran's main enrichment site, with a huge underground fuel enrichment plant and a pilot plant. Next door, the tunneling at Pickaxe Mountain is watched as a possible next-generation hardened site.
bases.assets: Underground Fuel Enrichment Plant; Pilot Fuel Enrichment Plant; power and support infrastructure; nearby Pickaxe Mountain tunnel complex.
bases.year: Struck on 2 and 21 March 2026 with bunker busters after June 2025 strikes; as of late May 2026 the underground plant was inaccessible, primary and backup power destroyed, and no sign of renewed enrichment. Pickaxe Mountain was not attacked and construction continues.

bases.name: Strait of Hormuz
bases.why: The narrow exit from the Persian Gulf between Iran and Oman's Musandam peninsula, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and a large share of its LNG normally pass. Closing it is Iran's ultimate lever, and in 2026 it pulled it.
bases.assets: Shipping lanes in Omani waters; Iranian islands, coastal missiles, mines and fast boats on the north shore.
bases.year: Iran blocked the strait in early March 2026 and later claimed sovereignty and demanded transit fees; the US imposed a counter-blockade of Iranian ports on 12-13 April. A June deal briefly lifted both blockades but collapsed on 8 July. Lloyd's List counted just 104 non-Iranian transits in the week of 5-11 October and at least 28 attacks in October, the worst month since the war began.

sources.label: Lloyd's List Intelligence: Strait of Hormuz Brief, 22 October 2026

bases.name: Bab el-Mandeb Strait
bases.why: The southern gate of the Red Sea, about 26 km wide between Yemen and Djibouti, through which all Suez traffic must pass. The Houthis have shown that a militia with drones and missiles can reroute global shipping around Africa.
bases.assets: Perim (Mayun) island splits the strait; Houthi anti-ship missiles and drones on the Yemeni coast; Western and Chinese naval bases in nearby Djibouti.
bases.year: The Houthis joined the Iran war on 28 March 2026, declared a blockade of Saudi shipping through the strait on 20 July, captured Mocha on 10 September and reached Dhubab on the strait opposite Perim on 11 September. Traffic held near normal (26 commodity ships on 10 September) but the threat level is the highest in years.

bases.name: Suez Canal
bases.why: The shortcut between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean that saves ships roughly two weeks versus sailing around Africa. Its value depends on the Bab el-Mandeb at the other end of the Red Sea staying open, which is why Houthi attacks hit Egypt's canal revenue so hard.
bases.assets: 193 km canal; Egyptian Navy and army forces along the canal zone.
bases.year: Traffic depends on the Red Sea; the Houthi advance to the Bab el-Mandeb in September 2026 renewed the threat to Suez-bound shipping.

sources.label: Container News: Houthis reach Bab el-Mandeb after seizing Mocha port

bases.name: Shimon Peres Negev Nuclear Research Center (Dimona)
bases.why: The heart of Israel's undeclared nuclear weapons program, with a heavy-water reactor and plutonium reprocessing according to open-source assessments. Iran has repeatedly tried to hit it, which makes it a flashpoint in its own right.
bases.assets: Research reactor and associated facilities; heavily defended by Arrow, David's Sling and Iron Dome.
bases.year: On 21 March 2026 Iran fired missiles at the center; they hit residential areas of Dimona town about 20 km away, injuring at least 47 people.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Shimon Peres Negev Nuclear Research Center

bases.name: Nevatim Airbase
bases.why: Home of Israel's F-35I Adir stealth fighters, the jets that lead long-range strikes on Iran. That makes it Iran's top military target in Israel.
bases.assets: F-35I Adir squadrons; transport and tanker aircraft.
bases.year: Iran's IRGC claimed strikes on Nevatim and Tel Nof on 8 June 2026; no impact was confirmed. Nevatim was also hit in Iran's 2024 missile barrages.

bases.name: Isfahan Nuclear Technology Center
bases.why: Iran's uranium conversion and fuel fabrication hub, plus a tunnel complex where enriched material is believed to have been stored. Conversion is the step that turns yellowcake into feed for centrifuges, so without Isfahan the enrichment chain breaks. Point is Isfahan city; the center lies southeast of the city.
bases.assets: Uranium Conversion Facility; Fuel Plate Fabrication Plant; research reactors; underground tunnel complex.
bases.year: Hit by Israel and the US in June 2025. In 2026 the tunnel complex was largely untouched, but its portals stayed backfilled with dirt as of May 2026, and a nearby Isfahan air base and ammunition depot were bombed on 30 March 2026.

sources.label: ISIS: Comprehensive Imagery Report on Nuclear Enrichment Related Sites, Post-April Ceasefire

bases.name: Hmeimim (Khmeimim) Air Base
bases.why: Russia's main air base in Syria, used to fly the bombing campaign that kept Assad in power and as a refueling stop for Russian flights to its forces in Africa. Its future after Assad's fall decides whether Russia keeps any real military reach in the Middle East and Mediterranean.
bases.assets: Russian combat and transport aircraft (reduced since 2024); air defenses; logistics hub for Russian operations in Africa.
bases.year: Under a Syria-Russia memorandum announced 9 August 2026, Syria takes over management of the airport and the military facilities become joint training and qualification centres, with a three-month transition.

sources.label: Al-Monitor/Reuters: Syria and Russia reach deal on future of Tartous and Hmeimim bases

bases.name: Tartus naval facility
bases.why: Russia's only naval repair and supply point on the Mediterranean, letting its warships operate there without sailing home through the Turkish Straits, which Turkey has closed to warships since 2022. Losing it would leave the Russian navy without a warm-water foothold in the region.
bases.assets: Piers, floating repair capacity and logistics for Russian Navy ships (presence sharply reduced since December 2024).
bases.year: The 9 August 2026 Syria-Russia memorandum hands the commercial berth and Pier No. 4 to Syrian control and turns military facilities into joint training centres, ending Russia's free hand at the port.

sources.label: Al-Monitor/Reuters: Syria and Russia reach deal on future of Tartous and Hmeimim bases

bases.name: Al-Tanf garrison
operators: formerly US Army and Special Operations Forces
bases.why: A desert outpost at the Syria-Iraq-Jordan border triangle that sat astride the Iran-to-Lebanon land route. For years it was a symbol of the US blocking Iran's 'land bridge' to Hezbollah.
bases.assets: Former US garrison and 55 km deconfliction zone; now Syrian army units.
bases.year: US forces fully withdrew on 11 February 2026 and moved to Jordan; CENTCOM confirmed the handover to Syrian forces on 12-13 February.

bases.name: Al Asad Airbase
bases.why: For two decades the largest US base in western Iraq, and the target of Iran's 2020 ballistic missile retaliation for the killing of Qasem Soleimani. Its handover marks the end of the US military era in Iraq.
bases.assets: Large airfield in Anbar province, now under Iraqi control.
bases.year: US withdrawal began in September 2025 and Iraqi forces took full control on 17 January 2026. The last US troops left Iraq on 29 September 2026.

sources.label: CSMonitor: After Iran war damage, US may close some Middle East bases for good

bases.name: Incirlik Air Base
bases.why: A NATO air base in southern Turkey within reach of Syria, Iraq and the eastern Mediterranean, and one of the European sites where open-source analysts say US B61 nuclear bombs are stored. Its use always depends on Ankara's mood, which makes it a barometer of US-Turkey relations.
bases.assets: Turkish 10th Tanker Base Command; US 39th Air Base Wing; reported B61 storage vaults.

bases.name: Kurecik Radar Station
bases.why: An AN/TPY-2 forward-based X-band radar in eastern Turkey that gives NATO early tracking of ballistic missiles launched from Iran. It cues the Aegis Ashore sites in Romania and Poland and US Navy destroyers.
bases.assets: AN/TPY-2 ballistic missile defense radar (NATO BMD system).

bases.name: RAF Akrotiri
bases.why: Britain's main air base in the eastern Mediterranean, inside a UK Sovereign Base Area on Cyprus. It has launched RAF strikes in Iraq, Syria and Yemen and supports intelligence collection across the Levant.
bases.assets: RAF Typhoon detachments; tankers and transports; intelligence and surveillance aircraft on rotation.
bases.year: Hit by a drone around 1 March 2026 during the Iran war.

bases.name: Souda Bay (NSA Souda Bay and Hellenic Navy base)
bases.why: A deep-water harbor on Crete with a NATO pier the US Navy says is one of the few in the Mediterranean able to berth an aircraft carrier alongside, plus an airfield for maritime patrol and ISR. It is the eastern Mediterranean's most useful US logistics stop.
bases.assets: Marathi NATO pier; Hellenic Navy base; airfield shared with Chania airport; US P-8 and ISR detachments.

bases.name: Camp Lemonnier
bases.why: The only permanent US military base in Africa, sitting on the Bab el-Mandeb next to Djibouti's airport. It supports counterterrorism in Somalia and Yemen and Red Sea operations, and it is a few kilometers from China's first overseas base.
bases.assets: Combined Joint Task Force Horn of Africa; special operations forces; airlift and drone operations (drones mostly at nearby Chabelley).

bases.name: PLA Support Base in Djibouti
bases.why: China's first overseas military base, opened in 2017 next to the Doraleh port. It supports Chinese anti-piracy and evacuation missions and is the model for how Beijing builds a global naval logistics network.
bases.assets: Fortified compound with a long pier able to berth large warships; PLA Navy marines and logistics units.

sources.label: Wikipedia: People's Liberation Army Support Base in Djibouti

bases.name: Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia
bases.why: A remote atoll in the middle of the Indian Ocean that lets US heavy bombers reach the Middle East and South Asia while staying beyond the range of most enemy missiles. Prepositioned supply ships here can equip a Marine brigade.
bases.assets: Long runway for B-52, B-1 and B-2 bombers; prepositioning ships; naval support facility and space tracking station.
bases.year: The UK allowed the US to use Diego Garcia for what it called 'defensive operations' in the 2026 Iran war; an Iranian missile attempt against it around 21 March was reported but not substantiated. On 11 April 2026 the UK put the Chagos handover treaty with Mauritius into the 'deep freeze' after Trump turned against it.

sources.label: Kuwait Times/AFP: UK puts Chagos handover deal in deep freeze after Trump criticism

bases.name: Berbera Airport
bases.why: One of the longest runways in Africa, built by the Soviets in the Cold War, on the Gulf of Aden in self-declared Somaliland. Its location near the Bab el-Mandeb makes it a prize for any power that wants to watch the Red Sea.
bases.assets: Roughly 4 km runway; deep-water port nearby.

bases.name: Gwadar Port
bases.why: The China-built deep-water port at the end of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, near the mouth of the Gulf of Oman. Analysts watch it as a possible future Chinese naval access point close to Hormuz.
bases.assets: Multipurpose berths run by a Chinese state firm; Pakistan Navy presence in the area.

bases.name: Ramstein Air Base
bases.why: The headquarters of US Air Forces in Europe and Africa and of NATO's Allied Air Command, and the main US airlift gateway to Europe, Africa and the Middle East. The 'Ramstein format' meetings that coordinated weapons for Ukraine were named after it.
bases.assets: HQ USAFE-AFAFRICA; NATO AIRCOM; 86th Airlift Wing (C-130J and VIP airlift); major passenger and cargo terminal; Landstuhl hospital nearby.

bases.name: Naval Station Rota
bases.why: A Spanish naval base just outside the Strait of Gibraltar that hosts forward-deployed US Aegis destroyers for NATO ballistic missile defense. It is also a key airlift stop between the US and the Middle East.
bases.assets: Forward-deployed US Navy Arleigh Burke-class destroyers (BMD); airfield for airlift and maritime patrol; Spanish fleet units.

bases.name: Aviano Air Base
bases.why: Home of the US 31st Fighter Wing in northern Italy and one of the NATO sites where open-source estimates place US B61 nuclear bombs. It flew combat missions over the Balkans in the 1990s and covers Southern Europe and the Mediterranean.
bases.assets: 31st Fighter Wing F-16C/D squadrons; reported B61 storage.

bases.name: Naval Air Station Sigonella
bases.why: The 'Hub of the Med' in Sicily, home to the maritime patrol and drone aircraft that watch the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Black Sea approaches. NATO's own Global Hawk surveillance fleet flies from here.
bases.assets: US Navy P-8A and MQ-4C Triton; NATO Alliance Ground Surveillance RQ-4D; logistics hub for 6th Fleet.

bases.name: Rzeszow-Jasionka Airport (Ukraine aid hub)
bases.why: An airport 70 km from the Ukrainian border that became the main transshipment hub for Western weapons going to Ukraine. Aid flown in is trucked along the A4 to the border, which makes it the single most important logistics node in Kyiv's war effort.
bases.assets: Cargo apron and logistics hub; Patriot air defense deployed since March 2022.

bases.name: Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base (57th Air Base)
bases.why: A Romanian base near Constanta on the Black Sea coast, used by US forces since 1999 and slated to become the biggest NATO air base in Europe. It anchors NATO's southeastern flank facing Crimea.
bases.assets: Romanian 57th Air Base and helicopter units; US Army rotational forces; planned major expansion.

bases.name: Aegis Ashore Redzikowo
bases.why: A land-based Aegis missile defense site on Poland's Baltic coast with SM-3 interceptors, part of NATO's shield against ballistic missiles from the Middle East. Moscow calls it a top-priority target because it sits so close to Kaliningrad.
bases.assets: Aegis Ashore (SPY-1 radar, Mk 41 launchers with SM-3 Block IB and IIA).

sources.label: Wikipedia: Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense System

bases.name: Aegis Ashore Deveselu
bases.why: The first Aegis Ashore missile defense site, operational in southern Romania since 2016, covering southern Europe against ballistic missiles from the Middle East.
bases.assets: Aegis Ashore (SPY-1 radar, Mk 41 launchers with SM-3 interceptors).

sources.label: Wikipedia: Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense System

bases.name: Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule)
bases.why: The northernmost US military base, halfway between Washington and Moscow on the polar route that Russian ICBMs would fly. Its radar gives early warning of missile launches and tracks objects in space, and it sits at the center of the fight over Greenland.
bases.assets: Upgraded Early Warning Radar (AN/FPS-132); satellite command and control; deep-water port and airfield.
bases.year: Under a US-Denmark-Greenland security agreement signed 22 September 2026, the US may modernize and enlarge Pituffik and open new defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, with free movement between them. The deal ended a year of Trump pressure to take the island outright.

sources.label: Euronews: Trump signs Greenland security deal allowing US to expand military presence

bases.name: Keflavik Air Base
bases.why: NATO's anchor in the middle of the GIUK gap, the sea passage Russian submarines must cross to reach the Atlantic. US Navy P-8 sub-hunters rotate here and NATO fighters take turns policing Iceland's airspace.
bases.assets: Rotational US Navy P-8A Poseidon; NATO air policing detachments; radar and command facilities.

bases.name: HMNB Clyde (Faslane)
bases.why: Home of Britain's entire nuclear deterrent: the Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines carrying Trident missiles, plus the Astute attack submarines. The nearby Coulport depot stores the warheads.
bases.assets: Vanguard-class SSBNs with Trident II D5; Astute-class SSNs; RNAD Coulport warhead storage.

bases.name: RAF Lakenheath
bases.why: The largest US Air Force fighter base in England, with F-15E Strike Eagles and the first US Air Force F-35A squadrons in Europe. It is USAFE's main long-range strike fighter base.
bases.assets: 48th Fighter Wing: F-15E and F-35A squadrons.

bases.name: RAF Fairford
bases.why: The US Air Force's main forward bomber base in Europe, with a long runway and facilities for B-52s, B-1s and B-2s. From here bombers can reach the Middle East and Russia's western flank.
bases.assets: Bomber Task Force deployments (B-52H, B-1B, B-2A); tanker support.
bases.year: Fourteen US bombers deployed here on 11 March 2026 for the Iran war, after about a dozen B-1Bs arrived in Europe around 9 March.

bases.name: RAF Fylingdales
bases.why: A ballistic missile early-warning radar on the Yorkshire moors, part of the same chain as Pituffik and Clear in Alaska. It watches for missiles launched toward the UK and US and tracks satellites.
bases.assets: Solid-state phased array early warning radar (Upgraded Early Warning Radar).

bases.name: RAF Menwith Hill
bases.why: One of the largest signals intelligence sites in the world, recognizable by its cluster of radomes. It is a ground station for US spy satellites and a key node in Five Eyes intelligence sharing.
bases.assets: Satellite ground station radomes; signals intelligence processing.

bases.name: Ile Longue SSBN base
bases.why: Base of France's four ballistic missile submarines, the sea leg of Europe's only independent nuclear deterrent outside Britain. With US commitments in question, France's deterrent has become a live European debate.
bases.assets: Triomphant-class SSBNs with M51 missiles; hardened submarine pens.

bases.name: Buchel Air Base
bases.why: Germany's NATO nuclear-sharing base, where open-source estimates place US B61 bombs for delivery by German jets in wartime. Germany is replacing its Tornados here with F-35As for this mission.
bases.assets: German Tornado wing (transitioning to F-35A); US munitions support squadron; reported B61 storage.

bases.name: Gibraltar (HM Naval Base and RAF Gibraltar)
bases.why: British base on the Rock that overlooks the Strait of Gibraltar, used by Royal Navy and US nuclear submarines and as an airfield for patrols over the strait.
bases.assets: Naval base and submarine berth; RAF airfield; signals intelligence.

bases.name: Baltiysk Naval Base (Kaliningrad)
bases.why: Main base of Russia's Baltic Fleet in the Kaliningrad exclave, wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Kaliningrad bristles with Iskander missiles and air defenses that can reach deep into NATO territory, making it both a threat and a hostage in any Baltic war.
bases.assets: Baltic Fleet surface combatants, corvettes and submarines; Kaliningrad region hosts Iskander-M brigades and S-400 air defense.

bases.name: Severomorsk (Northern Fleet HQ)
bases.why: Headquarters of Russia's most powerful fleet on the Kola Peninsula, which hosts most of Russia's sea-based nuclear forces. From here, submarines head for the Atlantic through the GIUK gap, the core problem NATO's northern flank is built to solve.
bases.assets: Northern Fleet HQ; Kirov-class battlecruiser and surface combatants; naval aviation at Severomorsk-1/3.

bases.name: Gadzhiyevo submarine base
bases.why: Home port of Russia's Northern Fleet ballistic missile submarines on the Kola Peninsula. These boats carry a large share of Russia's second-strike nuclear capability, hidden in the Barents Sea bastion.
bases.assets: Borei-class and Delta IV-class SSBNs with Bulava and Sineva SLBMs.

bases.name: Olenya Air Base
bases.why: An Arctic bomber base on the Kola Peninsula, used to launch cruise missile strikes on Ukraine from a site Russia thought was far beyond reach. Ukraine proved otherwise with Operation Spiderweb.
bases.assets: Tu-95MS and Tu-22M3 bombers (dispersed rotations); support aircraft.
bases.year: Hit in Operation Spiderweb on 1 June 2025, when truck-launched drones destroyed four Tu-95s and an An-12 here according to OSINT; overall the raid hit about 20% of Russia's operational long-range aviation per FT estimates.

bases.name: Engels-2 Air Base
bases.why: Russia's main strategic bomber base on the Volga, home to the Tu-160 Blackjack and Tu-95 Bear regiments that carry nuclear and conventional cruise missiles. Ukrainian long-range drones have repeatedly hit it and its fuel depots.
bases.assets: 121st Guards Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment (Tu-160M); 184th Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment (Tu-95MS).
bases.year: Ukrainian drones hit the base and its fuel depots several times in 2025, and Russian channels reported another drone attack with fires on 16 July 2026; damage was not confirmed.

sources.label: Kyiv Independent: Russia's Engels air base reportedly struck in Ukrainian drone attack

bases.name: Plesetsk Cosmodrome
bases.why: Russia's military spaceport in the far north, launching most of its military satellites and serving as a test site for ICBMs. Its high latitude suits polar and Molniya orbits used for reconnaissance and early warning.
bases.assets: Soyuz-2 and Angara launch pads; ICBM test launch silos and pads.

bases.name: Sevastopol Naval Base
operators: Russian Navy Black Sea Fleet (occupying force)
bases.why: Historic home of the Black Sea Fleet in occupied Crimea and the reason Russia seized the peninsula in 2014. Ukrainian missiles and sea drones have hit the fleet headquarters, dry docks and ships here, pushing much of the fleet east to Novorossiysk.
bases.assets: Black Sea Fleet HQ, piers and dry docks; air defenses; remaining surface ships and submarines.
bases.year: During Ukraine's August 2026 raid on Novorossiysk, Russian officials said 115 Ukrainian drones were shot down over Sevastopol.

sources.label: AAP via Newcastle Herald: Ukraine's blitz damages Russia's Black Sea stronghold

bases.name: Novorossiysk Naval Base
bases.why: Now the Black Sea Fleet's main base after Ukraine made Sevastopol too dangerous, and also a major oil export port including the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal. Zelensky calls it the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea.
bases.assets: Black Sea Fleet surface ships and Kilo-class submarines; Grushovaya oil terminal; CPC export terminal nearby.
bases.year: In August 2026 Ukraine hit the base with anti-ship missiles, jet drones and sea drones, targeting air defenses and piers; Russia claimed more than 500 drones downed across the region.

sources.label: AAP via Newcastle Herald: Ukraine's blitz damages Russia's Black Sea stronghold

bases.name: Kerch Strait and Crimean Bridge
bases.why: The narrow strait linking the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov, spanned by the 19 km Crimean Bridge that is Russia's road and rail link to occupied Crimea. Ukraine has attacked the bridge repeatedly because cutting it starves Crimea's garrison. The east shore is Russia; the west shore is occupied Ukrainian Crimea.
bases.assets: Crimean road and rail bridge; air defenses; ferry crossings.

bases.name: Bosporus (Turkish Straits)
bases.why: The only sea route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, running through Istanbul and governed by the 1936 Montreux Convention. Turkey closed the straits to belligerent warships in 2022, trapping Russia's Black Sea Fleet and keeping reinforcements out.
bases.assets: About 31 km strait, under 1 km wide at its narrowest; Turkish naval and coast guard control.

bases.name: Suwalki Gap
bases.why: A roughly 65 km strip of the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. If Russia closed it, the Baltic states would be cut off by land from the rest of NATO, which is why it is called NATO's Achilles heel.
bases.assets: NATO forward presence in Poland and Lithuania; German armored brigade being built up in Lithuania.

bases.name: GIUK Gap
bases.why: The sea gaps between Greenland, Iceland and the UK that Russian Northern Fleet submarines must pass to reach the Atlantic and NATO's supply lines. Cold War anti-submarine warfare was built around it, and it matters again. Point is a representative spot on the Iceland-Faroes ridge.
bases.assets: Seabed sensors, P-8 patrols from Keflavik and Lossiemouth, NATO attack submarines and frigates.

bases.name: Strait of Gibraltar
bases.why: The 14 km wide gateway between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Any navy moving between the two passes here, under the watch of Gibraltar, Rota and Morocco.
bases.assets: Shipping lanes under Spanish, British and Moroccan surveillance.

bases.name: Nagurskoye Air Base
bases.why: Russia's northernmost air base on Franz Josef Land, part of its Arctic military build-up. It extends Russian air defense and patrol coverage over the Arctic Ocean and the polar approaches to North America.
bases.assets: Arctic Trefoil base complex; runway for fighters and transports; air defense units.

bases.name: Vilyuchinsk (Rybachiy) submarine base
bases.why: Russia's Pacific ballistic missile submarine base on Kamchatka, giving direct access to the open Pacific. Point is the closed town of Vilyuchinsk; the Rybachiy base is on the adjacent bay.
bases.assets: Borei-class SSBNs; Oscar II and Yasen-class submarines.

bases.name: Dombarovsky (Yasny) air and missile base
bases.why: An air base next to the Strategic Rocket Forces' Dombarovsky missile field in the southern Urals, where open-source reporting says Russia deployed its first Avangard hypersonic glide vehicles. It shows where Russia is fielding its newest strategic weapons.
bases.assets: Heavy ICBM silos (open-source reporting: Avangard on UR-100N UTTKh); air base.

bases.name: US Fleet Activities Yokosuka
bases.why: Headquarters of the US Seventh Fleet and home of the only US aircraft carrier based outside the United States. It lets the US keep a carrier strike group days rather than weeks from a Taiwan or Korea crisis.
bases.assets: Seventh Fleet flagship; forward-deployed carrier (USS George Washington) and Destroyer Squadron 15; ship repair facility; JMSDF Fleet HQ next door.

sources.label: Wikipedia: United States Fleet Activities Yokosuka

bases.name: US Fleet Activities Sasebo
bases.why: Home of the US Navy's forward-deployed amphibious ships in Japan, which carry Marines from Okinawa. It sits on the Korea Strait and the East China Sea.
bases.assets: Forward-deployed amphibious assault and landing ships; mine countermeasures ships; fuel and ammunition depots.

sources.label: Wikipedia: United States Fleet Activities Sasebo

bases.name: Kadena Air Base
bases.why: The largest US air base in the Pacific, on Okinawa about 700 km from Taiwan. It is the 'Keystone of the Pacific' for any air campaign over the Taiwan Strait, and also the most exposed to Chinese missiles.
bases.assets: 18th Wing: rotational fighters (F-15EX planned), KC-135 tankers, E-3 AWACS, HH-60 rescue; Navy P-8s; Army Patriot battalion.

bases.name: Misawa Air Base
bases.why: A joint US-Japan air base in northern Honshu that faces Russia's Far East and the Sea of Japan. Its fighters specialize in suppressing enemy air defenses, and Japan bases its own F-35As here.
bases.assets: 35th Fighter Wing F-16CM (US); JASDF F-35A wing; Navy patrol and signals intelligence units.

bases.name: Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni
bases.why: One of the densest concentrations of US combat aircraft in Asia, home to the Yokosuka carrier's air wing when ashore and to Marine F-35B squadrons. It gives the US a fifth-generation strike force within range of the Korean Peninsula and East China Sea.
bases.assets: Carrier Air Wing 5 (F/A-18E/F, EA-18G, E-2D); Marine Aircraft Group 12 with F-35B; KC-130J tankers.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni

bases.name: Yonaguni Island garrison
bases.why: Japan's westernmost island, only about 110 km from Taiwan. Its coastal surveillance and electronic warfare units watch Chinese ships and aircraft moving around Taiwan, and it is part of Japan's missile 'wall' along the Ryukyu chain.
bases.assets: JGSDF coastal observation unit and radar; electronic warfare unit; planned air defense missile unit.

bases.name: Camp Humphreys
bases.why: The largest US overseas military base by area, south of Seoul, housing the headquarters of US Forces Korea, United Nations Command and Eighth Army. It is the command center for any war on the Korean Peninsula.
bases.assets: HQ USFK, UNC and Eighth Army; 2nd Infantry Division elements; Army aviation; Desiderio Army Airfield.

bases.name: Osan Air Base
bases.why: Headquarters of US Seventh Air Force and home of the 51st Fighter Wing, the closest permanent US fighter base to North Korea. It also hosts U-2 spy planes that watch the North.
bases.assets: Seventh Air Force HQ; 51st Fighter Wing (F-16, A-10 being retired); U-2S detachment; Patriot batteries.

bases.name: Yulin Naval Base (Sanya, Hainan)
bases.why: China's key South China Sea naval base on Hainan, with tunnels cut into the hillside for submarines and home to Jin-class ballistic missile submarines. Deep water just offshore lets those submarines slip into the South China Sea bastion.
bases.assets: Type 094 Jin-class SSBNs; attack submarines; underground submarine pens; nearby carrier pier for the Shandong.

bases.name: Woody Island (Paracel Islands)
bases.why: China's administrative and military hub in the Paracels, also claimed by Vietnam and Taiwan. China has deployed HQ-9 surface-to-air missiles and fighters here, making it the northern anchor of its South China Sea defenses.
bases.assets: Runway and hangars; HQ-9 SAM deployments (reported since 2016); port; Sansha administrative center.

bases.name: Fiery Cross Reef
bases.why: One of China's three big artificial island air bases in the Spratlys, built on a reef also claimed by Vietnam, the Philippines and Taiwan. It has a 3 km runway, hangars for fighters and bombers, radars and missile shelters, turning a submerged reef into an unsinkable carrier. Point is the reef; the base is on its southwest end.
bases.assets: 3,000 m runway; hardened hangars; radar and sensor arrays; harbor; reported anti-ship and air defense missile shelters.

bases.name: Subi Reef
bases.why: A Chinese-built artificial island air base in the northern Spratlys, about 25 km from Philippine-held Thitu (Pag-asa) Island. Its runway and lagoon port let China keep forces constantly near Philippine outposts.
bases.assets: About 3,000 m runway; hangars; large lagoon harbor; radar and communications.

bases.name: Mischief Reef
bases.why: A Chinese artificial island base inside the Philippines' exclusive economic zone, which the 2016 arbitral tribunal ruled is a low-tide elevation China cannot claim as territory. It is the logistics hub for China Coast Guard pressure on Second Thomas Shoal nearby.
bases.assets: About 2,700 m runway; hangars; lagoon harbor; China Coast Guard and maritime militia staging.

bases.name: Scarborough Shoal
bases.why: A rich fishing atoll about 220 km off Luzon, inside the Philippines' EEZ but under China Coast Guard control since a 2012 standoff. If China ever built an island here, it would put a base within easy reach of Manila and Subic Bay, which is why Washington treats it as a red line.
bases.assets: No permanent structures; China Coast Guard and maritime militia presence.
bases.year: China held military and coast guard drills near the shoal on 1 August 2026 after water-cannon clashes with Philippine vessels, and has issued nature-reserve rules for it.

sources.label: China Global South/AFP: China says it conducted military, coast guard drills near disputed shoal

bases.name: Second Thomas Shoal (Ayungin)
bases.why: A reef where the Philippines deliberately grounded the rusting WWII-era BRP Sierra Madre in 1999 and keeps a handful of Marines aboard. Chinese attempts to block resupply missions here are the most likely trigger for invoking the US-Philippine defense treaty.
bases.assets: BRP Sierra Madre with a small Marine garrison; Philippine resupply boats.
bases.year: Resupply runs under a provisional arrangement agreed in July 2024. In April 2026 the Philippines accused China of using cyanide around the atoll.

bases.name: Kinmen Islands
operators: Republic of China Army Kinmen Defense Command
bases.why: Taiwan-held islands only a few kilometers off China's city of Xiamen, shelled heavily in the 1950s Taiwan Strait crises. They are the most likely target for a limited Chinese 'gray zone' squeeze or blockade short of full invasion.
bases.assets: Kinmen Defense Command garrison; coastal defenses; Taiwan coast guard.
bases.year: During China's Justice Mission 2025 drills on 29-30 December 2025, flights to Kinmen and Matsu were blocked, affecting about 6,000 travelers.

bases.name: Matsu Islands
operators: Republic of China Army Matsu Defense Command
bases.why: Taiwan-held islands off the Chinese coast near Fuzhou, dependent on undersea cables and ferries that China can easily disrupt. They are a test case for Chinese coercion that stops short of war.
bases.assets: Matsu Defense Command garrison; undersea communications cables.
bases.year: The China Coast Guard announced patrols near Matsu and Wuqiu during Justice Mission 2025 on 29-30 December 2025.

bases.name: Taiwan Strait
bases.why: The roughly 130 to 180 km stretch of water between China and Taiwan, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes and the most dangerous potential war zone on the planet. Any invasion or blockade of Taiwan starts here.
bases.assets: PLA amphibious, naval, air and rocket forces on the mainland side; Taiwanese anti-ship missiles, mines and air defenses on the other.
bases.year: Justice Mission 2025 (29-30 December 2025) was the eighth major PLA drill around Taiwan since 2022, with live-fire zones inside Taiwan's territorial waters for the first time since 2022, 27 rockets fired from Pingtan, and simulated blockades of Keelung and Kaohsiung.

bases.name: Luzon Strait (Bashi Channel)
bases.why: The gap between Taiwan and the Philippines that PLA Navy ships and submarines use to reach the western Pacific. Whoever controls the islands on either side can open or shut that door, which is why the US and Philippines have built up forces in the Batanes and northern Luzon.
bases.assets: Philippine Batanes islands; Taiwan's southern bases; major undersea cables.

bases.name: Pratas Island (Dongsha)
bases.why: A tiny Taiwan-held atoll about 300 km from Hong Kong and far from Taiwan itself. It sits on the approach to the Bashi Channel, and analysts see it as a likely first target if Beijing wanted a low-cost demonstration of force.
bases.assets: Airstrip; coast guard garrison.

bases.name: Taiping Island (Itu Aba)
bases.why: The largest naturally formed island in the Spratlys, held by Taiwan and also claimed by China, Vietnam and the Philippines. It has an airstrip and pier, giving Taipei a seat in the South China Sea dispute.
bases.assets: About 1,200 m runway; pier; coast guard garrison.

bases.name: Yongbyon Nuclear Scientific Research Center
operators: North Korean General Department of Atomic Energy
bases.why: The heart of North Korea's nuclear weapons program, where plutonium has been produced since the 1980s and uranium is enriched. Activity here is the best open indicator of how fast Pyongyang is growing its arsenal.
bases.assets: 5 MWe graphite-moderated reactor; experimental light water reactor; uranium enrichment plant; reprocessing facility.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Nyongbyon Nuclear Scientific Research Center

bases.name: Sohae Satellite Launching Station
bases.why: North Korea's main space launch center on the west coast, where it launched its first military reconnaissance satellite. Space launches double as tests of long-range missile technology.
bases.assets: Launch pads and engine test stands; recently expanded coastal launch complex.

bases.name: Andersen Air Force Base
bases.why: America's main bomber and munitions hub in the western Pacific, on US soil in Guam rather than in an ally's territory. It is the launch pad for long-range strikes in a Taiwan war and a primary target for China's DF-26 'Guam killer' missiles.
bases.assets: 36th Wing; rotating Bomber Task Force deployments (B-52H, B-1B, B-2A); large fuel and munitions storage; tankers and ISR.

bases.name: Naval Base Guam (Apra Harbor)
bases.why: The westernmost US naval base on American soil, home to forward-deployed attack submarines that would hunt Chinese ships in a Pacific war. Marines are relocating some forces here from Okinawa.
bases.assets: Submarine Squadron 15 (forward-deployed attack submarines); submarine tender; ammunition wharf; Marine Corps Camp Blaz nearby.

bases.name: Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam
bases.why: Headquarters of the US Pacific Fleet and Pacific Air Forces, a short drive from INDOPACOM headquarters. It is the command and repair heart of US military power in the Pacific.
bases.assets: Pacific Fleet HQ; PACAF HQ; attack submarines; destroyers; shipyard; Hawaii ANG F-22s and C-17s; KC-135s.

bases.name: RAAF Base Darwin
bases.why: Australia's northern gateway facing Southeast Asia and the South China Sea, hosting the yearly US Marine Rotational Force-Darwin and visiting US bombers. It puts US and Australian forces within reach of the first island chain.
bases.assets: RAAF fighter and surveillance deployments; US Marine Rotational Force-Darwin; US bomber and tanker rotations.

bases.name: RAAF Base Tindal
bases.why: An inland air base in Australia's Northern Territory being upgraded so US B-52 bombers can deploy here, beyond the range of most Chinese missiles while still able to strike the South China Sea.
bases.assets: RAAF F-35A squadron; new apron and facilities for US bomber deployments; fuel storage.

bases.name: HMAS Stirling (Garden Island)
bases.why: Australia's main Indian Ocean naval base near Perth and the home of AUKUS: from 2027 up to four US Virginia-class and one UK Astute-class nuclear submarines are due to rotate through here under Submarine Rotational Force-West.
bases.assets: All six Collins-class submarines; Anzac-class frigates; replenishment ship; nuclear submarine support infrastructure under construction.
bases.year: Visiting nuclear attack submarines are building toward the 2027 rotations: USS Minnesota (February-March 2025), USS Vermont (October-November 2025) and HMS Anson (February-March 2026).

bases.name: Pine Gap (Joint Defence Facility)
bases.why: A joint US-Australian satellite ground station in the desert near Alice Springs that controls signals-intelligence satellites and relays missile launch warnings. It covers much of Asia and the Middle East, which makes it one of the most important intelligence sites on Earth.
bases.assets: Dozens of radomes; signals intelligence satellite ground control; missile early warning relay.

bases.name: Ream Naval Base
bases.why: A Cambodian base on the Gulf of Thailand rebuilt with Chinese money, with a new pier able to take large warships. Chinese warships have berthed here repeatedly, and Washington sees it as China's second overseas base in all but name, close to the Strait of Malacca and the South China Sea.
bases.assets: New deep-water pier and dry dock built with Chinese funding; Cambodian patrol vessels; visiting PLA Navy corvettes.
bases.year: An AP report in January 2026 said the US littoral combat ship USS Cincinnati was making a friendship visit to Ream, a rare US call at the China-upgraded base.

sources.label: Washington Times/AP: USS Cincinnati making friendship visit to Cambodia's Ream naval base

bases.name: Strait of Malacca
bases.why: The main shipping lane between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, carrying a huge share of world trade and most of China's imported oil. Beijing's fear of a blockade here, its 'Malacca dilemma', drives much of its naval and port strategy.
bases.assets: About 800 km long, narrowing to under 3 km at the Singapore Strait; patrolled by littoral states; US Navy rotations at Singapore's Changi.

bases.name: Hambantota International Port
bases.why: A Sri Lankan port leased to a Chinese state company for 99 years in 2017 after Colombo struggled with its debts. Sitting beside the main Indian Ocean shipping lane, it is the classic example in the 'debt-trap' basing debate and a worry for India.
bases.assets: Deep-water port leased to China Merchants; occasional Chinese research and survey vessel calls.

bases.name: Coco Islands
bases.why: Myanmar islands just north of India's Andaman Islands, where satellite imagery has shown a lengthened runway and new structures. India worries they could give China a listening post overlooking Indian missile tests and the approaches to Malacca.
bases.assets: Extended airstrip; radar and support buildings reported in imagery.

bases.name: Andaman and Nicobar Command (Port Blair)
bases.why: India's only tri-service theater command, on islands that sit at the western mouth of the Strait of Malacca. It gives India a natural position to watch or block Chinese shipping heading into the Indian Ocean.
bases.assets: Naval base at Port Blair; air stations at Car Nicobar and Campbell Bay; army brigade; coast guard.

bases.name: INS Kadamba (Karwar)
bases.why: India's large new west coast naval base under Project Seabird, designed to host aircraft carriers and dozens of warships away from congested Mumbai. It strengthens India's hold on the Arabian Sea opposite Pakistan.
bases.assets: Breakwater-protected harbor; ship lift; berths for carriers and surface combatants.

bases.name: PAF Base Nur Khan
bases.why: Pakistan's main air transport and VIP base in Rawalpindi, next to army headquarters and close to the command of its nuclear forces. An Indian strike here in May 2025 showed how quickly an India-Pakistan crisis can reach nuclear-sensitive ground.
bases.assets: Transport, tanker and VIP aircraft; airborne early warning support.
bases.year: Struck by Indian missiles on 10 May 2025 during the India-Pakistan conflict.

bases.name: Naval Station Norfolk
bases.why: The world's largest naval base, home port of the Atlantic Fleet's carriers and the headquarters behind US Navy operations from the Arctic to the Mediterranean. NATO's only command headquartered in the US also sits here.
bases.assets: US Fleet Forces Command and Second Fleet; multiple Nimitz- and Ford-class carriers; cruisers, destroyers and amphibious ships; NATO Allied Command Transformation.

bases.name: Naval Base San Diego
bases.why: The principal home port of the US Pacific Fleet's surface ships, with carriers based across the bay at North Island. Most US warships that deploy to the Western Pacific start here.
bases.assets: Destroyers, cruisers, amphibious ships and littoral combat ships; nearby NAS North Island carriers and Point Loma submarines.

bases.name: Naval Station Roosevelt Roads (Ceiba, Puerto Rico)
bases.why: A former Cold War naval air station in eastern Puerto Rico, closed in 2004 and brought back to life as the forward hub for US operations against Venezuela. It shows how fast the US can reopen a mothballed base when a new theater heats up.
bases.assets: Reactivated runway and taxiways; up to 20 F-35s supported by Vermont ANG's 158th Wing; AC-130J gunship seen at the field; logistics for Operation Southern Spear.
bases.year: Reactivation visible in October 2025 and officially back in operation on 14 November 2025. F-35As were photographed here after the 3 January 2026 raid that captured Nicolas Maduro.

bases.name: Guantanamo Bay Naval Base
bases.why: The oldest US overseas base and the only one in a country with which Washington has no friendly relations, held under a 1903 lease Cuba rejects. It overlooks the Windward Passage and houses the military detention center and a migrant operations center.
bases.assets: Naval station and airfield; detention facility; migrant operations center.
bases.year: The Trump administration began sending migrants to the base in early 2025; legal challenges continued.

bases.name: Panama Canal
bases.why: The shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific that US warships and a big slice of US trade depend on. Trump's 2025 threats to 'take back' the canal over Chinese influence made it a political flashpoint again.
bases.assets: Locks at both ends; Balboa and Cristobal ports; US treaty right to defend the canal's neutrality.
bases.year: In early 2026 Panama's high court voided Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison's port concessions, and the Panama Maritime Authority took over Balboa and Cristobal ports on 23 February 2026. Traffic rose up to 10% after the Iran war as US LNG carriers rerouted to Asia, but drought cut daily transits to 32 by 15 September 2026.

bases.name: Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay
bases.why: The Atlantic home of US Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines, half of the sea leg of the US nuclear triad. It also hosts the Trident refit and missile handling facilities for the East Coast.
bases.assets: Ohio-class SSBNs with Trident II D5; Ohio-class guided missile submarines; Trident Refit Facility.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay

bases.name: Naval Base Kitsap (Bangor)
bases.why: The Pacific home of most US ballistic missile submarines and their Strategic Weapons Facility, near Seattle. It keeps the Pacific half of the US sea-based nuclear deterrent on patrol.
bases.assets: Ohio-class SSBNs with Trident II D5; Strategic Weapons Facility Pacific; Seawolf-class attack submarines; Puget Sound shipyard nearby.

bases.name: Whiteman Air Force Base
operators: US Air Force Global Strike Command
bases.why: The only operational home of the B-2 Spirit stealth bomber, the one aircraft able to carry the GBU-57 bunker buster. Any US strike on deeply buried targets anywhere in the world can fly nonstop from Missouri.
bases.assets: 509th Bomb Wing and Missouri ANG 131st Bomb Wing (B-2A Spirit); Air Force Reserve 442nd Fighter Wing (A-10).
bases.year: B-2s from Whiteman dropped GBU-57 bunker busters on Fordow and Natanz on 22 June 2025 (Operation Midnight Hammer), the first combat use of the weapon.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2025 United States strikes on Iranian nuclear sites

bases.name: Francis E. Warren Air Force Base
operators: US Air Force Global Strike Command
bases.why: Headquarters of Twentieth Air Force, which runs all US land-based ICBMs, and home of a Minuteman III wing whose silos are spread across Wyoming, Nebraska and Colorado. It is set to be the first base for the new Sentinel ICBM.
bases.assets: 90th Missile Wing (Minuteman III in 150 silos); Twentieth Air Force HQ.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Francis E. Warren Air Force Base

bases.name: Cheyenne Mountain Space Force Station
bases.why: The famous nuclear bunker carved into a granite mountain near Colorado Springs, now the alternate command center for NORAD and US Northern Command. It is built to keep missile and air warning running even after a nuclear attack.
bases.assets: Hardened underground complex on blast springs; NORAD/USNORTHCOM alternate command center; missile warning and space surveillance links.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Cheyenne Mountain Space Force Station

bases.name: Buckley Space Force Base
bases.why: A base in Aurora, Colorado that runs the US space-based infrared satellites that detect missile launches worldwide. When Iran or North Korea fires a ballistic missile, the first warning often comes through here.
bases.assets: Space-based infrared missile warning mission control; satellite ground stations (radomes); Colorado ANG F-16s.

bases.name: Fort Greely (Ground-based Midcourse Defense)
bases.why: The main US homeland missile defense interceptor field in interior Alaska, built to stop a limited ICBM attack from North Korea. It is the backbone that the planned Golden Dome system would build on.
bases.assets: Ground-Based Interceptors in silos; Alaska Army National Guard missile defense battalion.

bases.name: Fuerte Tiuna (Fort Tiuna)
operators: Bolivarian National Armed Forces of Venezuela
bases.why: Venezuela's main military complex in Caracas, housing the Defense Ministry and command headquarters. It was the focus of the US raid that captured Nicolas Maduro, a rare case of a capital's main military base being hit in a decapitation operation.
bases.assets: Defense Ministry and army HQs; armored units (Dragoon 300 vehicles seen destroyed); air defense sites.
bases.year: Struck on 3 January 2026 in Operation Absolute Resolve, when about 150 US aircraft hit air defenses and bases across northern Venezuela and Army special operations helicopters captured Maduro in Caracas. Satellite imagery showed destroyed buildings, gate facilities and armored vehicles here.

sources.label: The War Zone: Destruction seen at Caracas base that was a focus of the US military operation
